page_title: A Survey of Memory Bandwidth and Machine Balance in Current High Performance Computers

sources.entry: Memory Bandwidth and Machine Balance in Current High Performance Computers - Defines sustainable bandwidth as what unit-stride loops get, not bus peak, and machine balance as flops per access.

summary.title: A Survey of Memory Bandwidth and Machine Balance in Current High Performance Computers
summary.one_liner: Machine balance defined as peak floating-point ops per cycle divided by sustained (uncached, unit-stride) memory ops per cycle, with a STREAM-based survey showing most hierarchical-memory machines sustain only a small fraction of their peak bandwidth.
takeaways: Machine balance here is defined using sustained unit-stride memory bandwidth rather than peak memory ops, to avoid bias from cache miss penalties.
The STREAM benchmark (four long vector operations in Fortran 77) was used to measure sustainable bandwidth, which vendors rarely published.
Hierarchical-memory shared-memory systems typically sustained only 5-10% of the memory bandwidth needed to keep floating-point pipelines busy.
Vector machines had low balance (about one load or store per flop) and were more cost-effective on STREAM TRIAD performance than cached systems.
Codes slower than STREAM TRIAD are likely memory-bandwidth bound; faster ones (super-streaming) are likely CPU-bound.
summary.summary: McCalpin surveys sustainable memory bandwidth and machine balance across uniprocessor, vector, shared-memory and distributed-memory computers of the mid-1990s. He defines balance as peak floating-point ops per cycle over sustained memory ops per cycle, measured with the STREAM benchmark on unit-stride vector operations. Results are grouped by memory system type and plotted against STREAM TRIAD MFLOPS, with trend data for DEC, HP, IBM, SGI and Cray machines and a case study on a 2D ocean model. The paper concludes that hierarchical-memory designs need architectural changes such as prefetch and cache bypass to tolerate latency.
